tier_reason: First-party README Benchmarks table (2017) with CPU models stated (2x Xeon E5-2697 2.7GHz; Core i7-3667U) and competitor scripts in examples/keras, examples/tensorflow, examples/tiny-dnn, but the compiler, its version and the flags used for the runs are not stated (the Makefile only defaults to gcc -O2), so not A; no independent measurement, so not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks table (first-party, 2017). mnist-mlp, Linux 1 CPU: KANN+SSE 31.3 s, KANN+BLAS 18.8 s versus Theano+Keras 33.7 s (KANN+BLAS about 1.8x, KANN+SSE about 1.08x, derived from page data), Tiny-dnn 2m19s (KANN+SSE about 4.4x, derived) and Tiny-dnn+AVX 1m34s (about 3.0x, derived). Mac 1 CPU: KANN 27.1 s versus TensorFlow 33.4 s and Theano+Keras 37.2 s. mul100-rnn, Linux 4 CPUs: KANN+SSE 12m13s and KANN+BLAS 8m18s versus Theano+Keras 19m52s (about 1.6x and 2.4x, derived); 1 CPU: KANN+SSE 40m05s is slower than Theano+Keras 27m30s, KANN+BLAS 22m58s is about 1.2x faster (derived). mnist-cnn, 4 CPUs: KANN 19m09s versus Theano+Keras 24m24s (about 1.27x, derived); 1 CPU: KANN 57m57s versus Tiny-dnn+AVX 300m40s (about 5.2x, derived) but slower than Theano+Keras 37m12s.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from 2017 (Theano 0.8.2, Keras 1.2.2, TensorFlow 1.0.0, Tiny-dnn pulled March 1 2017), long before current frameworks; compiler version and flags used for the README runs are not stated, so tier C although the competitor scripts are in the repo (examples/keras, examples/tensorflow, examples/tiny-dnn). The README itself says not to read too much into the table, that Theano is about 50% faster than KANN single-threaded because of MKL sgemm, and that MKL/OpenBLAS matmul can be twice as fast as KANN's own. Without BLAS, KANN loses single-threaded to Theano+Keras on both mnist-cnn (57m57s vs 37m12s) and mul100-rnn (40m05s vs 27m30s); its wins are against Tiny-dnn, on multi-threaded rows (better intra-batch threading than Theano+Keras), and on the KANN+BLAS rows that add OpenBLAS-0.2.19, so the claim is not that KANN's own kernels beat MKL. TensorFlow was measured only on the Mac. None of the baselines are in the category's incumbent list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor). Last commit 2025-06-06 (NEON support); no commits between April 2021 and June 2025.

notes: README numbers and hardware match the record; added the Tiny-dnn+AVX and 1-CPU mul100-rnn rows, which show KANN without BLAS losing single-threaded to Theano+Keras. Metadata checked on github.com: MIT (LICENSE.txt, Dana-Farber/Broad), 761 stars, not archived, last commit 2025-06-06 (stale). Shortcomings: 2017-era baselines, unstated build, single-thread losses to MKL-backed Theano.

tier_reason: First-party folly::Benchmark results pasted into the source comment of thrift/lib/cpp2/protocol/benchmark/ThriftProtocolBenchmarks.cpp (run 2025-11-18, buck2 mode/opt-clang-lto); code is public but the CPU model, clang and protobuf versions are not stated and the build is Meta-internal, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Source comment 'Results for last run: 2025-11-18', time per iteration. Serialize Small: Thrift Binary 380.11 ns, Compact 395.36 ns, CurSe 230.85 ns versus Protobuf Array 945.69 ns, String 832.30 ns, ZeroCopy 998.08 ns (Binary about 2.2-2.6x faster, derived from page data). Serialize Medium: Binary 936.16 ns, Compact 948.40 ns, CurSe 456.09 ns versus Protobuf 2.94 us / 2.55 us / 3.04 us (Binary about 2.7-3.2x, derived). Serialize Large: Binary 2.72 us, Compact 2.75 us, CurSe 1.23 us versus Protobuf 9.54 us / 8.32 us / 9.60 us (Binary about 3.1-3.5x, derived). The CurSe serialize rows skip building the struct (see caveats), so their 3.6-4.3x over Protobuf is not like-for-like. Deserialize Small: Binary 396.13 ns, Compact 424.35 ns, CurSe 427.60 ns versus Protobuf 660.66-681.08 ns (Binary about 1.7x, derived). Deserialize Medium: Binary 1.06 us, Compact 1.10 us versus Protobuf 2.08-2.18 us (about 1.9-2.1x, derived). Deserialize Large: Binary 3.15 us, Compact 3.29 us versus Protobuf 6.58-6.68 us (about 2.1x, derived).
corrections.caveats: First-party results pasted into a source comment (dated 2025-11-18); the benchmark code is public but CPU model, core count, clang and protobuf versions are not stated, and it needs the Meta fbcode/buck2 build (mode/opt-clang-lto), so it is not reproducible as published (tier C). Serialize benchmarks build the test object inside the timed loop for Thrift Binary/Compact and Protobuf (createThriftTestData / createProtobufTestData run every iteration), so the ratios mix object population with encoding, and population is not symmetric: Thrift copy-assigns the prebuilt std::vector and std::map, while Protobuf appends the 10 list elements one by one and inserts the 5 map entries one by one into a protobuf Map. The CurSe serialize rows write the constants straight to the cursor writer with no struct built at all, so CurSe-vs-Protobuf serialize ratios are not like-for-like, and the CurSe deserialize row discards what it reads (no doNotOptimizeAway). Deserialize runs exclude serialization via BenchmarkSuspender; the Protobuf String path copies the IOBuf into a std::string inside the timed region, while the Array path parses in place. Protobuf SerializeToArray writes directly into a pre-sized IOBuf (no extra copy); only the SerializeAsString row adds a copyBuffer copy. No protobuf Arena is used. One tiny synthetic schema (i32, i64, 8-byte string, list<i32> of 10, map<string,i32> of 5, bool, double per group; 1, 3 or 9 groups), no realistic string lengths. fbthrift is Facebook's branch of Apache Thrift (GitHub does not mark it a fork; is_fork_of left null).

notes: All time/iter numbers in the record match the source comment exactly; corrected the caveats: SerializeToArray does not copy, Protobuf population inserts list and map entries one by one while Thrift copies prebuilt containers, and CurSe serialize builds no object, so its 3.6-4.3x is not like-for-like. Metadata from github.com: Apache-2.0, 2.7k stars, not archived, last commit 2026-10-07 (active). Shortcomings: first-party, Meta-internal build, unstated CPU and protobuf version, asymmetric object population inside the timed serialize loop.

tier_reason: The source is a third-party peer-reviewed paper (SIGGRAPH 2026, arXiv 2605.06408, ACM DOI 10.1145/3799902.3811229) that would support B, but arxiv.org, research.chalmers.se, research.zenseact.com, emergentmind and themoonlight were all EGRESS_BLOCKED, so its tables were seen only as WebSearch snippets; capped at C per the snippet-only rule.

corrections.baseline: CGAL 3D Delaunay / regular triangulation, single-threaded and CGAL Parallel; the paper also has SciPy, Voro++, HXT (Gmsh) and gDel3D (GPU) columns
corrections.hardware: CPU methods on 16 cores of an AMD EPYC 9534 (WebSearch snippet only; GPU not captured)
corrections.workload: Runtime of 3D Voronoi / Delaunay construction on synthetic white-noise and density-gradient point sets and of power-diagram (weighted, regular triangulation) construction on clustered point sets, 0.1M to 15M points, plus real-world neural-rendering point sets, in a third-party SIGGRAPH 2026 GPU Voronoi paper (Taveira, Lindstrom, Fatemi, Hammarstrand, Kahl) that uses SciPy, CGAL, CGAL Parallel, Geogram, Voro++ and HXT as CPU baselines on 16 cores.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (paper not opened). Clustered weighted point sets, Geogram on 16 cores versus single-threaded CGAL: 100k points 0.060 s vs 0.449 s (about 7.5x, derived); 500k 0.250 vs 2.299 (about 9.2x); 1M 0.413 vs 4.808 (about 11.6x); 15M 5.890 vs 74.723 (about 12.7x), but these ratios compare 16 threads with one thread. Against CGAL Parallel on the same 16 cores the gap is far smaller: white noise 15M points, Geogram 6.138 s vs CGAL Parallel 6.903 s (about 1.12x, derived from snippet data); clustered 100k points, Geogram 0.060 s vs CGAL Parallel 0.533 s. HXT (Gmsh) beats Geogram at scale: 2.259 s at 15M points, white noise (Geogram about 2.7x slower, derived from snippet data); the paper calls HXT the best CPU baseline, closely followed by Geogram.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: arxiv.org, research.chalmers.se (full-text PDF), research.zenseact.com (project page), emergentmind.com and themoonlight.io are blocked in this environment, so the paper (Taveira, Lindstrom, Fatemi, Hammarstrand, Kahl, 'Scalable GPU Construction of 3D Voronoi and Power Diagrams', SIGGRAPH 2026, arXiv 2605.06408, ACM DOI 10.1145/3799902.3811229) was not opened; the numbers come from WebSearch result text summarising its tables. CPU baselines ran on 16 cores of an AMD EPYC 9534 (snippet); compiler, flags, thread settings, Geogram and CGAL versions are unknown. The headline 7.5-12.7x compares 16-thread Geogram with single-threaded CGAL; against CGAL Parallel on the same cores Geogram is only about 1.12x faster at 15M white-noise points (6.138 s vs 6.903 s). The clustered table is power-diagram (weighted) construction, not plain Delaunay. Geogram is not the fastest CPU code in the comparison: HXT (Gmsh, already listed) took 2.259 s at 15M points, and the HXT paper reports a serial kernel about 3x faster than Geogram. The paper's purpose is a GPU method, with Geogram and CGAL as baselines. Geogram's own README and wiki pages carry no numbers.

notes: Every paper host and mirror tried (arxiv.org, research.chalmers.se PDF, research.zenseact.com, emergentmind, themoonlight) returned EGRESS_BLOCKED; 5 WebSearch queries confirmed the record's clustered numbers, the AMD EPYC 9534 16-core CPU setup, and same-core CGAL Parallel numbers. Claim corrected: the 12.7x is 16 threads vs 1 thread, the like-for-like gain over CGAL Parallel is about 1.12x at 15M points, and HXT (already listed) is about 2.7x faster than Geogram. baseline_in_list set true (CGAL is a geometry-spatial incumbent). Retier to B is possible if the paper PDF becomes reachable. Metadata from github.com: BSD-3-Clause, 2.6k stars, not archived, last commit 2026-10-06 (active).
